#9872. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 3): Attention is all you profile

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:

The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace shows the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

From the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that issue and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:

So attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

Before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:

Figure 1 shows the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the new operations are easy to spot:

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually launched.

Figure 2 shows the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

The in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up quickly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

Out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

We just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:

This one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:

Normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) shows why the alarm bells ring, the math backend launches 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 launched with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

In Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?"

The kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

In the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:

On the GPU this shows up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):

A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

Put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend launches only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

This is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

Let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

FlashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

Here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

Blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

If you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

And that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

By now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

Flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

No transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

It launches through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

The "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the plan (the "knob" search) on every call.

Fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

On the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

State out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

Profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗

Thanks to Noe Flandre for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗

Thanks for the series, really delightful!

#9871. The State of Python Profiling in 2026

p403n1x87@heliopolis:~/posts/the-state-of-python-profiling-in-2026$ ▮

$ cat the-state-of-python-profiling-in-2026.md

Fri 30 October 2026 26 min read programming/ #python #profiling #optimisation

CPython now ships its own sampling profiler, free-threading is going mainstream, and coding agents have started reading profiles. In this post I look at where Python profiling stands today, compare Tachyon, py-spy, Scalene and Austin, and go through what's new in Austin 4.1.

Python profiling has changed more in the last two years than in the decade before. CPython 3.14 gave external tools an official way to look inside a running interpreter, and made asyncio task graphs inspectable from outside the process. CPython 3.15 ships a sampling profiler in the standard library. Free-threaded builds have gone from experiment to something people actually deploy. And a growing share of the people reading profiles aren't people at all, but coding agents.

This post looks at where things stand: what the main sampling profilers can do today, where each one fits, and what changed in the latest release of Austin.

As many of you know, I've been working on Austin for the best part of eight years now, so I have a view from the inside on how this landscape came to be, and, naturally, a soft spot for one of the tools in it. I've tried to be fair to the others: what I say about them comes from their own documentation and release notes as of October 2026. If I've got something wrong, let me know and I'll fix it.

Most profilers make two basic choices, and these choices explain most of the differences between tools.

Tracing or sampling. A tracing (deterministic) profiler like cProfile records every function call and return. You get exact call counts, but the overhead changes the program's timing, sometimes a lot. A sampling profiler looks at the call stack at regular intervals and builds a statistical picture from those snapshots. You don't get call counts, but the program runs at close to normal speed. I went into the differences between the two, and how they work under the bonnet, in an earlier post.

In-process or out-of-process. An in-process profiler runs inside your program, usually by starting it for you or being imported. An out-of-process profiler is a separate program that reads the target's memory from outside. Out-of-process tools can attach to something that's already running, like a production server that started misbehaving an hour ago, without restarting it or changing its code.

All four tools in this post are sampling profilers. Tachyon, py-spy and Austin work from outside the process. Scalene works from inside.

There are many more Python profilers than I can cover here, so I've picked the ones I think are the most widely known and used, and that have a track record on accuracy and overhead. That track record isn't just my opinion. The most thorough comparison of Python profilers I know of, by the Scalene team at UMass Amherst (Berger, Stern and Altmayer Pizzorno, 2022), measured a dozen of them on the longest-running benchmarks of the pyperformance suite. Its conclusion was that sampling profilers are "both more efficient and often more accurate" than tracing ones.

The two go together. A tracing profiler runs its own code on every function call and return, inside your program, so it slows the program down, and not evenly: code that makes many small calls is slowed down far more than code that makes few, which skews the picture of where time is spent. The study found one tracing profiler reporting that a function took 80% of the run time when it actually took 25%. A sampling profiler stays out of the way of your code, so the timings it reports are much closer to how the program behaves when nobody is watching. In the study, Austin, py-spy and Scalene were among the profilers with the lowest overhead in CPU mode, adding between 0% and 2% to the run time, compared with 73% for cProfile and more than 200% for some others.

Tracing profilers still have their place: they count every call exactly, which sampling can't do. If you need to know that a function was called 1,204 times, use cProfile. If you need to know where the time goes, sample.

Tachyon is too new to have been part of that study, but as the profiler that now ships with Python, it's the one many people will reach for first, so it belongs here.

One notable absence is pyflame, Uber's profiler from 2016. It was one of the first to sample Python stacks from outside the process, and it deserves credit for showing that the approach works. But it was Linux-only, its last changes date from 2019, before Python 3.8 was released, and its repository is now archived and marked as no longer maintained. I mention a few other good tools at the end of the post.

With a sampling profiler, the time attributed to a function is an estimate: the fraction of samples it appears in, multiplied by the duration of the run. Like any statistical estimate, its error shrinks as the number of samples grows, roughly in proportion to 1/√n. Sampling 10 times faster gives you about three times less noise from the same run, so short runs give stable results and short-lived functions are less likely to be missed entirely.

So the maximum rate a profiler can sustain, without disturbing the target, directly limits how accurate it can be.

That's why raw sampling speed has been a priority for Austin from the start, and it's the reason it's written in C and does nothing but sample: every microsecond saved per sample is another sample per second. Each release has pushed this further. Austin 4.0 more than doubled the maximum sampling rate of 3.x, and 4.1 pushes it higher again (more on that below), with a default of 10,000 samples per second.

Tachyon's authors clearly think the same way: the profiler is named after the hypothetical particle that travels faster than light. Its sampling core is written in C too, and while its default rate is a more conservative 1,000 samples per second, it's designed to be raised well beyond that. When a profiler that's been around since 2018 and the one that has just joined the standard library both put speed first, it's a good sign that sampling rate is finally getting the attention it deserves.

Profiling Python from outside the process used to be close to a hack. CPython made no promises about the layout of its internal structures, so tools like Austin and py-spy had to copy large parts of the interpreter's private headers for every Python version, and work out where the interesting fields were from compiler- and platform-specific details. Every new release could break them, and often did.

Those tools showed that the approach was worth it. Being able to attach to a running process with no instrumentation and almost no overhead turned out to be winning proposition in production, and evidently it made a strong case for CPython to support out-of-process tools properly, rather than just tolerate them.

Some of that work came directly from Austin. In 2021, I made three changes to CPython, each to solve a problem I'd run into while working on Austin:

Tachyon reads both co_qualname and native_thread_id today. In 2023 I moved the fields that out-of-process tools rely on to the top of the interpreter's structures (gh-105271). That change was one of the references Pablo Galindo cited when he proposed the debug offsets table (gh-106597): a structure at the start of the runtime state that tells external tools where to find the data they need, without copying any headers. I later added more fields to it (gh-121311). The debug offsets table is the foundation that PEP 768's remote debugging interface is built on, and that Tachyon uses to read the interpreter's state.

So the profiler that now ships with CPython is, in a sense, the result of years of external tools proving that out-of-process sampling works. CPython made it a supported use case, and the core developers have now built a sampling profiler into the interpreter itself. I find that very satisfying, and it's good news for every external tool too, Austin included.

The biggest news of the year is that CPython 3.15 includes a sampling profiler, profiling.sampling, also known as Tachyon (it was proposed alongside reorganising cProfile into profiling.tracing, in PEP 799). It builds on the remote debugging support added in 3.14 by PEP 768.

Tachyon covers a lot of ground for a first release:

The obvious advantage is that it's already there: nothing to install, and it's maintained alongside the interpreter, so it stays in step with internal changes.

The main limit is version coverage. Tachyon only profiles Python 3.15 and later, and the profiler and the target must run the same minor version (and the same build type: free-threaded or standard). If your services run on 3.12, Tachyon doesn't help you yet. Its --native option adds placeholder frames to show where Python calls into native code, but doesn't unwind the native stack itself.

If you've used Austin, much of Tachyon will feel familiar. The basic approach of reading the interpreter's memory from outside the process is shared with py-spy, and goes back to pyflame in 2016. But beyond that, many of the features Tachyon has added since its first commit in August 2025 are ones Austin has had for years:

Some of these exist in py-spy too, and it goes the other way as well: Tachyon's asyncio support landed before Austin's. That's how open source should work, with good ideas spreading between projects. What's missing is the credit. PEP 799 doesn't mention Austin, py-spy or any of the external profilers whose approach Tachyon adopts. I think that's a missed opportunity to recognise the years of community work that came before the standard library caught up, and that made it possible.

py-spy, written in Rust, made out-of-process sampling mainstream for Python, and it's what many people mean when they say "Python sampling profiler".

Its record, top and dump commands are a model of a simple interface. It writes SVG flame graphs, Speedscope and Chrome trace files, can follow subprocesses, filter to threads holding the GIL, and include or exclude idle threads. With --native it also unwinds native C, C++ and Rust frames on Linux (x86_64 and, since recently, aarch64) and Windows.

py-spy 0.4.2, released in April 2026, added Python 3.14 support. At the time of writing, free-threaded builds aren't supported yet (there's an open issue tracking it), and there's no task-aware asyncio mode: coroutines appear as ordinary frames on whichever thread runs the event loop.

Scalene takes a different approach. It runs your program for you and profiles from the inside, which lets it measure things external tools can't easily see.

Its strengths are breadth and line-level detail:

Two of these numbers come with caveats. Scalene doesn't observe native code directly: it uses a timer signal, and treats any delay in handling it as time spent in native code, during which Python can't handle signals. But CPython only handles signals on the main thread, so in a program with several busy threads the delay can simply come from waiting for its turn on the GIL. In 2022, Pablo Galindo showed a multi-threaded, pure-Python program that Scalene reported as spending most of its time in native code (scalene#428). Scalene's author replied that worker threads are profiled in a different way, but the issue is still open, and the current code still estimates the main thread's native time from the signal delay. So treat the Python/native split with some care in multi-threaded programs.

For GPU time on NVIDIA, Scalene needs the GPU's per-process accounting mode, which has to be enabled once with root privileges. Without it, Scalene falls back to the utilisation of the whole GPU, including other processes, and shows a warning saying so.

Scalene 2.4 (October 2026) supports free-threaded Python 3.13 and 3.14. By its own figures, the overhead is typically 10–20%. That's fine during development, but the trade-off of being in-process is that you can't attach Scalene to something already running. You have to start the program under it.

Austin is the tool I maintain. It's a frame stack sampler written in pure C, with no dependencies beyond the C standard library and the operating system. It reads the interpreter's memory from outside the process, writes every sample to a compact binary format called MOJO, and leaves the analysis to other tools. Because it doesn't aggregate anything while it samples, it can sample very fast.

Austin 4.1 supports CPython 3.10 through 3.15, including free-threaded builds, on Linux, macOS and Windows. On Linux it also runs on less common architectures like i686, armv7 and ppc64le. Each release drops the oldest Python versions, but older releases of Austin are still available if you need to profile something older: Austin 4.0 supports 3.9 through 3.14, 3.7 supports 3.8 through 3.13, and 3.5 goes all the way back to Python 2.3.

Austin 4.1 adds four things worth covering in some detail.

Austin 4.0 already more than doubled the maximum sampling rate of the previous release, by cutting down how much memory Austin reads from the target and how much work it does to write each sample. 4.1 goes further: Austin now detects when a thread's stack hasn't changed since the previous sample. When that happens, it skips walking the stack again and writes a short "same as before" marker instead of the whole stack, which also makes the output files smaller. It also buffers its output instead of writing each sample separately.

Every performance change to Austin is benchmarked in CI against the code it replaces, and the results are posted on the pull request. Here are the two that made the biggest difference, measured on Linux (x86_64) with Python 3.13, at the smallest sampling interval (1 µs), where Austin samples as fast as it can:

In CPU time mode, where Austin also has to check whether each thread is on the CPU, the same changes took the maximum rate from 20,000 to 32,000 samples per second (+60%) and from 34,000 to 37,000 (+9%) respectively.

Something to keep in mind is that the gain from repeated stack detection depends on how often stacks repeat between samples. That happens a lot when a program spends time in long-running loops or calls, but it varies with the workload.

As explained earlier, this matters for accuracy: at the default 100 µs interval, Austin collects up to 10,000 samples per second per thread, ten times Tachyon's default rate.

With -n/--native, Austin collects native call stacks and interleaves them with the Python frames they belong to:

This shows, for example, what's actually happening inside NumPy, a Cython module or a Rust extension built with PyO3, not just that time was spent "somewhere in native code". In native mode Austin also samples threads that never run Python code, like worker threads started by native libraries, which are invisible to profilers that only look at Python threads.

Austin users may remember that native stacks used to need a separate tool, austinp, a variant of Austin that uses libunwind to walk native stacks. It was a separate tool for two reasons. It only worked on Linux. And it broke one of Austin's founding principles, minimal impact on the program being profiled: to walk a thread's native stack reliably, libunwind needs the thread to stand still, so austinp had to stop each thread while sampling it. I wrote about that trade-off in Spy on Python down to the Linux kernel level.

The new native mode fixes the first problem. It works on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64), macOS and Windows (x86_64), with no extra dependencies, because Austin now walks native stacks itself instead of relying on libunwind. Its design owes a lot to samply, Markus Stange's excellent native sampling profiler, which showed how fast and portable this kind of unwinding can be. On macOS, Austin captures native stacks the same way samply does. On Linux, both unwind using the compiler-generated unwind tables, though they capture stacks differently, and on Windows samply relies on the system's event tracing while Austin unwinds stacks itself. As far as I know, Austin is currently the only out-of-process Python profiler that unwinds native stacks on macOS. austinp is still available on Linux, for the architectures that native mode doesn't cover yet and for sampling kernel stacks.

There is one other way to get Python and native frames in the same profile. Since 3.12, CPython can make Python function calls visible to native profilers like perf and samply (on macOS from Python 3.15), if you enable its perf support with -X perf or PYTHONPERFSUPPORT=1. You get Python function names in a fully native profile. But it has to be enabled inside the target process, it only goes down to functions, not lines, and it slows Python down: in 2023 Mark Shannon measured an 8% slowdown on a standard build, with more expected in builds that keep frame pointers. So it's a good option for a quick look at a local program, rather than for attaching to something already running.

The second problem is a deliberate compromise. To get a consistent native stack, Austin still has to briefly suspend each thread while sampling it, so native mode has more impact on the program than Austin's normal mode, and the impact grows with the sampling rate. Use a larger interval (1 ms is a good start), and avoid it in production. That's why native mode is an option you turn on, not the default. In its normal mode, Austin still never pauses the program it's profiling, and I explained the reasoning behind that in an earlier post.

On CPython 3.14 and later, Austin tracks the asyncio task graph: each event loop's tasks, the coroutine chain each task is executing or suspended at, and which tasks are awaiting which. Samples are attributed to the task running on the thread, and the stacks of suspended tasks are recorded together with the await relationships between them.

That's what you need to answer the question that ordinary flame graphs get wrong for async code: not "which frames were on the CPU", but "which task was slow, and was it slow because it was working or because it was waiting on something else?" And austin -w prints the live task tree of a running application, grouped under the thread whose event loop owns it.

There's a further difference that's easy to miss. Most sampling profilers only record what was running, so each sample is anonymous: they can tell you that fetch_user took 30% of the time, but not whether that was one slow task or a thousand quick ones. Tachyon's async-aware mode labels each stack with the name of its task, but still adds the samples up into a single aggregate profile. Austin records which task each sample belongs to, and follows each task from the first time it sees it to the last. That makes its asyncio support closer to a tracer in spirit, while keeping the low overhead of sampling.

The VS Code extension makes use of this. Alongside the usual flame graph, which adds up time across all tasks, its Task Trace panel shows a flame chart for each event loop: every task drawn from when it was first seen to when it was last seen, nested under the task awaiting it, with how much of that time it spent running and how much waiting. So you can see what happened over time, not just where the time went in total, which is often what you need to work out why a request was slow.

Here's an uncomfortable truth: most Python code never gets profiled. Not because the tools are missing, but because profiling feels hard to get into. You have to pick a tool, run it the right way, and then make sense of a flame graph full of frames you've never heard of. Many developers try it once, feel lost, and go back to guessing. That's a shame, because as I argued in How to bust Python performance issues, a single profiling run often turns up easy wins. A big part of what I want Austin to do is lower that barrier, and 4.1 approaches it from two directions.

Let an agent do the work. Coding agents can now profile code with Austin and reason about the results themselves. You ask "why is this endpoint slow?", and the agent runs Austin, finds the hot path, proposes a fix, and profiles again to check that the fix worked. There are two ways to set this up:

The command line is a good place to start, but agents get more out of the Python API behind it. Each query returns typed objects rather than text, so the agent can write a short script that hands them over to other libraries: pandas to compare two profiles, a plotting library to chart the results, or the project's own code to work out which component owns each hot function. An analysis that would take a long chain of CLI calls, each one reading the profile again, becomes a few lines of Python over a profile loaded once. The selectors and filters are the same as on the command line, e.g. q.filter(thread="main").callers("db.py:execute"), so the agent can move from one to the other without learning anything new. For example, this is all it takes to see which functions got faster, or slower, after a fix:

A word of caution, though: a single pair of profiles is a shaky basis for a verdict. Sampling, and the system itself, add noise from one run to the next, so part of the change above could be nothing more than that. For a rigorous answer, pyrometry is a small library of mine that implements the ideas of On the Algebraic Properties of Flame Graphs. It treats flame graphs as vectors that can be added, subtracted and averaged, and it compares two sets of profiles, say five runs before a change and five after, with a statistical test (Hotelling's T²), keeping only the stacks whose difference is significant. The result is then split into the stacks that appeared, disappeared, grew or shrank. That's out of reach for a chain of CLI calls, but it's a short script for an agent with the Python API, and pointing it at pyrometry gives it a sound method to follow instead of eyeballing two flame graphs. Nor is this just theory: Austin's own CI uses the same test to validate every pull request. It profiles the same scenarios ten times with the base branch and ten times with the changes, on every supported version of Python, and checks that the new build still reports the same data as the old one.

Or let it teach you. Having an agent fix things for you is useful, but it doesn't make you any better at reading a profile. So the MCP server also has action tools that let the agent search and zoom the flame graph in the editor, while you watch. That turns the extension into a learning tool: instead of "fix this", you can ask your agent to walk you through the analysis. It can zoom into the hot path and explain why it's hot, point out the frame where your code hands over to a library, or show you what time spent waiting looks like compared with time spent computing. You're both looking at the same flame graph, so after a few sessions you start to recognise the patterns yourself, and the next time, you might not need to ask. Busting performance issues, AI edition shows both approaches on a real project, including one of these guided tours.

The rest of the release is about meeting Python where it's going, and where it actually runs. Austin 4.1 supports Python 3.15 on day one, and free-threaded builds too. Free-threading changes a lot for a profiler: without the GIL, threads really do run at the same time, so a sampler has to keep up with all of them at once. The one thing it costs is some accuracy in memory mode, since without the GIL there's no reliable way to tell which thread caused a change in memory usage (see below).

Profiles are also easier to read. Threads now show up under the names you gave them in the threading module, so you see MainThread and worker-3 rather than a list of opaque thread IDs, which makes a big difference in a busy multi-threaded application.

Finally, a lot of Python runs in containers, and profiling it from the host used to be awkward. Austin 4.1 handles containerised processes better, and it now records the target's working directory, virtual environment and PYTHONPATH alongside the samples. That's the information a tool needs to map the file paths in a profile back to the source files on your machine, even when the code ran somewhere else.

Whilst Austin has a memory mode, users must be aware that it isn't an allocation profiler. Its memory mode measures changes in resident memory (RSS) between samples: how much physical memory the process is actually using, not how much it has asked for. These can be very different numbers. If you allocate a 512 MB array but only write to half of it, the operating system only provides physical memory for the half you've used, so RSS grows by about 256 MB.

That's exactly the test the Scalene study used to compare memory profilers: allocate 512 MB, touch between 0% and 100% of it, and check that the profiler reports 512 MB. Austin mostly reported less, and the study counted that as inaccurate. But reporting only the memory that was touched is the correct answer for what Austin measures. The study was asking an allocation question, and Austin answers a residency question. Both are useful: RSS tells you what your process really costs the machine, which is what matters when you're about to run out of memory. But if you want to know which line allocated what, or hunt for leaks, you want an allocation profiler like Scalene or memray. Austin also has no line-level GUI of its own. It relies on the VS Code extension, the TUI, Speedscope or pprof for visualisation, so out of the box it asks a bit more of you than Scalene or py-spy do. And attaching to a process needs elevated privileges on Linux and macOS, as it does for any out-of-process profiler.

There isn't one best profiler. Here's how I'd choose:

Other tools worth knowing about: pyinstrument for a friendly in-process call tree, memray for serious memory work, and cProfile (now profiling.tracing) when you need exact call counts.

Python profiling has never been in better shape. Having a sampling profiler in the standard library raises the baseline for everyone, and the remote debugging work in 3.14 and 3.15 makes all external tools more reliable. I expect the next round of progress to come from two directions: better support for concurrency (free-threading and asyncio together), and making profiling accessible to everyone, whether that means an agent doing the work or an agent teaching you to do it yourself. The best profiler is the one people actually use.

Austin 4.1 is available on PyPI, Homebrew, Snap, Chocolatey, Scoop, conda-forge and as standalone binaries from GitHub releases. The documentation covers everything above in more detail. If you try it, I'd love to hear how it goes.

#9870. Royal London plans IT outsourcing shake-up as staff brace for redundancies

IBM deal could see tech jobs shipped to India, with cuts expected before Christmas

Royal London plans to cut hundreds of IT jobs and shift work to India under an outsourcing deal with IBM, according to sources, with redundancies expected by the end of December.

Sources said Royal London's chief technology officer, James Sandell, told IT staff in September that the insurance and pensions giant was partnering with IBM to outsource a substantial portion of its technology operations. A consultation process was expected to follow.

A Royal London spokesperson told The Register: "Royal London has appointed IBM as its strategic technology infrastructure partner as it continues to develop its technology strategy. The partnership will give Royal London access to IBM’s specialist capability, scale and experience. Royal London will remain accountable for service delivery and regulatory requirements and continues to focus on ensuring continuity and quality of service for customers."

We asked Royal London how many UK IT roles it would retain and whether IBM would move work to India.

The exact number of jobs at risk remains unclear, although one Glassdoor review posted on October 6 claims that hundreds of positions in the company's technology operations division are being eliminated.

"A vast amount of knowledge is being lost by the business, a lot that is not yet documented due to constant years of recruitment freeze and workload volume," they wrote.

The reviewer also questioned whether management had grasped just how much work would be involved in handing operations over to IBM, particularly with already stretched teams being cut to a fraction of their former size.

Royal London replied to the Glassdoor review, acknowledging staff concerns about the changes, though it didn't comment on the claims about outsourcing and redundancies.

"We recognise that as Royal London is going through a period of transformation, this has raised questions and concerns for some colleagues," the company wrote. "We have established channels for colleagues to raise these, including through People Leaders and Colleague Representatives, and I encourage colleagues to use these routes to discuss their concerns."

Other October reviews questioned the handling of the outsourcing and Royal London's commitment to its mutual values.

An October 12 reviewer identifying themselves as an IT infrastructure employee said the company had historically offered good career prospects, before criticizing its new direction.

"Sudden outsourcing goes against all Royal London values," the reviewer wrote, adding that employees were questioning the company's direction amid reports of a hiring freeze and further potential cuts.

Another review, posted on October 20, suggested the IBM deal was the latest in a series of outsourcing decisions following an earlier move to transfer servicing jobs to South Africa.

"A mutual company but not mutual values when it comes to things like this," the reviewer claimed.

The planned cuts follow rising profits. Royal London reported adjusted group operating profit of £187 million in the first half of 2026, up 13 percent year-on-year.

Royal London has been keen to trumpet the benefits of its mutual structure, under which it is owned by customers rather than shareholders. Reporting the results in August, chief executive Barry O'Dwyer highlighted the £199 million distributed to eligible customers through ProfitShare in April.

"As a customer-owned business, when we do well, our customers share in that success," O'Dwyer said.

For employees facing redundancy before Christmas, the benefits of that success may be somewhat harder to appreciate.

#9869. Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

#9868. SAP promises to open out data flows in both directions

New commitment to Apache Iceberg and expanded Databricks partnership point to battle ahead over context layer

SAP has taken meaningful steps in opening its data to bidrectional sharing across the enterprise, and in decoupling the advanced analytics needed for AI from its ERP upgrade path.

During a technical conference last week, the German software giant adopted native support for Apache Iceberg, the open table format, and extended its partnership with Databricks to bring data from legacy ERP systems into its modern cloud analytics platform.

"By putting [a] stake in the ground with Iceberg, we now have SAP moving from a very closed application storage model to an open lakehouse model," said Aaron Rosenbaum, Gartner senior director analyst, referring to the concept which brings together data lakes and warehouses.

Also important was the bridge between modern analytics in the cloud and on-prem or hosted legacy systems such as ECC, the ERP system broadly adopted by global companies. "SAP made a pretty big move in saying we're going to open this up, not just to S/4HANA Cloud [the latest ERP system], but ECC users. That coupling — leveraging of AI, leveraging a lakehouse for AI to the ERP upgrade lifecycle — was a problem," said Rosenbaum.

In May this year, SAP bought Dremio, a lakehouse platform built around Apache Iceberg, ending its previous preference for Databricks' Delta Sharing to bring together SAP data products with existing lakehouses bi-directionally.

At SAP's TedEd conference last week, SAP said its Business Data Cloud (BDC) – the "trusted data foundation for SAP Business AI Platform" – would now support native Apache Iceberg and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris, "providing an open and governed data foundation for users and [AI agent platform] Joule to consume data."

Together with SAP BDC Connect, the new tech policy will support platform interoperability with "zero-copy data sharing" across platforms from Databricks, Snowflake, Google, AWS, and Microsoft. The system would also continue to support Delta Lake, the alternative open table format from Databricks, SAP said.

With the integration of Dremio's SQL query engine, BDC users will also get access to relational databases including SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without moving data, the vendor said.

During the same conference, Databricks – the lakehouse company born out of an Apache Spark platform – extended its partnership with SAP based on the previously announced SAP Databricks, which embeds the Databricks Data + AI Platform in BDC.

That "expanded scope" promises to make data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. The vendor said that a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, for example, could use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring historic order data into SAP Databricks, combining it with third-party data, and allowing data engineers to build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines. They can keep that work as they move to the cloud, Databricks suggested.

This being 2026, the hoped-for output from all of this data engineering is not just business insight, but automated action, by way of AI agents. SAP has its Joule AI assistant and agentic platform, while Databricks has Genie, and the two companies have promised to bring them together.

The increasing openness is good for users who will get more options in plotting a strategy to bring together enterprise data, leaving them pondering over where to put the business context layer, which vendors will no doubt fight to control, Rosenbaum said.

"You have the comment that they're going to bring Joule and Genie together in the future. This is pointing to a struggle that's going on throughout enterprises and throughout all the vendors about the context layer. I don't necessarily see that there's one winner. You do have different points of context within the transaction system and across the whole business, and they have been points of tension.

"Lack of single vendor lock-in is important. It's something that all the customers are struggling with: how do we build these context layers and deliver sort of consistent answers?"

SAP's shift in the direction of openness is likely to help users in this struggle, whether they choose to build the context layer within the ERP vendor's data platform using its semantic layer, or outside of it using tools from other vendors – there are plenty of companies offering help for those opening their wallets.

Nonetheless, whichever path users choose, a lot of work lies ahead. ®

#9866. GNU Mes and the 0.28 release

From the series: GNU Mes interpreter speedup

It’s been a while since the latest blog post in the series but we have been working very hard behind the scenes 1. This means I’ll probably forget a few things from all we did, but there’s a good reason for that: we were making a release.

This is the first official and serious release I make as a (co-)maintainer, and the whole thing makes me uncomfortable. Even though people treat me as an expert programmer sometimes, there are many things in programming that I struggle a lot with. The first one, that I think I improved on in the last few years, is writing software from scratch. The second is delivering things to people.

This is normal, as all my career has been focused on R&D and that’s the way I’ve been trained to work. In the case of this specific release, something inside me still thinks my most valuable contribution was that: the idea and demonstration that this attempt could work.

Most of my career has been based on learning in a short time period the right amount of information so I can achieve a reasonable result. Then I normally move on to the next project.

Thinking about that, trying to read through my feelings, I started to realize more and more that whatever that drives me is pushing me to somewhere else, maybe to those parts I struggle more with…

Releasing code is important. It’s the only way to make people actually enjoy the result of your work. I have no problem to admit I struggle with this.

As an R&D guy I’ve always considered myself an “enabler”. I do something, I show how it is done and let people learn from it and actually implement it. That’s fine in some contexts but it has been driving me to some level of frustration recently, as the size of the projects I take part in grow.

An example of this is the RISC-V bootstrap on Guix. I spent a couple of years of my life working on it. We made a working bootstrap for live-bootstrap. But it’s not yet included in Guix because I delegated the final step. Now, even after the years I spent on that, all the sleepless nights and everything, it’s something I cannot enjoy fully2, and you cannot enjoy at all.

This “my job here is done” mentality is not enough for me anymore.

The kind of projects I do now deserve something else. I deserve better.

In Mes I had like 300 commits in a branch, pretty ugly, doing, undoing and redoing some stuff over and over again. The whole codebase was upside down, the commit messages were sometimes good and sometimes lacking, I had fixup commits that fixed things that were changed so much the amount of conflicts the reordering produced was overwhelming… It was a mess. It was me trying new things, learning and cleaning things up as I went. My arborescent thought process at its fullest.

In my usual way of doing things, I decided to promise NlNet a release, something I’ve never done before 3.

Once the bytecode adventure was done, showing some good performance improvement was possible and that Janneke made me a co-maintainer, it was the only acceptable thing to do.4

But, if I wanted to do it, I would need to slow down.

In the last part of the bytecode adventures, you remember how we included Popsyntax, and we reworked the whole macro expansion game. That wasn’t me, but Tim Sample.

I don’t remember very well how he joined my efforts here but I guess I bothered him with questions because he’s a long term Mes contributor and he’s also the author of Popsyntax, the Germ scheme implementation and many interesting things more.

He decided to start over. Chose a Mes release and walked through my steps. Removed the macro expander from the internals and wrote one in Scheme. From there, the direction was set.

I worked through the huge branch that I had, removing the stuff that turned out to be unnecessary, and he took over the git history, and made sure that every single commit was working.

I cannot imagine how many conflicts the guy has been resolving. But damn this looks good now.

This week, I released GNU Mes 0.28. The first release that I do as a GNU maintainer.

Janneke has been guiding me through the whole process — including the part of publishing the website to GNU using CVS5. I’m sure I would’ve never been able to figure out everything on my own. What a ride it has been!

But after more than a year of work, I’m very happy that most of the comments on the release have been positive, specially the ones from people that I worked with and I have a huge respect for.6

But, what’s will you find in GNU Mes 0.28 that we didn’t mention in the blog yet?

First of all, the main difference from the earlier blogpost is now Mes can be compiled with both M2-Planet and MesCC, and also with GCC as before.

It’s a tricky process, because the error reporting is very limited (I’m being benevolent here), and I was being a very nasty boy with some gotos inside switch statements. After some wrestling with allowed C sintax, I figured it out.

M2-Planet is limited, and we had to leave some things out. When Mes is compiled with M2-Planet it doesn’t have support for errors (aka exceptions) and those abort the interpreter, this is because M2-Planet’s C library doesn’t include setjmp. The stack operations had also to be rewritten as functions for M2-Planet, as the macros with array access were too complex for it. With that, Mes is a little bit slower when compiled with M2-Planet.

None of those are a big deal because that’s only the starting point of the bootstrap process and Mes is rebuilt with MesCC right after it.

The 0.28 release has been tested on real RISC-V hardware that I have access to,7 uncovering a few issues here and there in the Mes C Library.

First, the assembly parts that take care of program initialization in RISC-V (written by myself a few years ago, when I was working on the bootstrap) were broken.

setjmp and longjmp that we use for error handling in Mes, and were not used before, are also faulty. Because of this, the RISC-V version of Mes in the bootstrap, when built with MesCC that is, does not support errors until the issue is fixed.

I also found some extra stuff because GCC 14 decided that implicit function declaration warnings should become errors, breaking the bootstrap that we didn’t test in a very long time in RISC-V, first, because hardware unavailability and, second, because Qemu is also faulty for RISC-V.

There is still a known issue with M2-Planet-built Mes that explodes when it calls strcpy, this can be triggered running (procedure-disassemble map) in the REPL. We didn’t manage to fix this yet.

Tim reworked the macro expansion and made a simple and understandable initial macro expander in Scheme.

With that ready, many things started to fall off naturally.

Most of our driving issues simply disappeared. The macro expander takes the steering wheel from the start, giving us zero garbage collection issues during boot.

The earlier macro expander I wrote in C had to also drive execution, which could possibly call the garbage collector, killing all the C pointers that we had. The new macro expander does everything from Scheme, so no pointers are lost: gc_preserve and gc_release are gone. The boot-done! mark is gone, too.

As Tim started from scratch, all the API is way cleaner, and our initial driver is as simple as:

We can now use the stack for preservation, as it doesn’t happen that often, and the initial driver is a minimal loop that iterates through the few top-level expressions the initial boot file has (the macro expander). The rest of the program is run from Scheme.

Continuing with macro expansion, even if in previous posts we talked about Popsyntax integration, we decided to leave that out the release for now. We focused on having a faster interpreter with a new VM.

Keeping macro expansion simple, we are faster than ever.

These are the updated numbers from the 0.28 release comparing with the previous 0.27.2 bugfix release, released a week before.

This is running in my Tuxedo laptop from 2020:

You can see the times are similar to the nosyntax (it’s basically the same) branch we described in the previous post.

Take in account the numbers are tricky because mescc-mes means Mes building itself running MesCC. From one version to the other Mes changed, making it a little bit larger (+200 LoC), which means it should take longer to compile. The new version overcomes that, and even achieves a 40% reduction on execution time.

The fib benchmark is the most savage to me. There you can easily see how running has become way cheaper. On the other hand, mescc-hello shows how building a small hello-world program is more expensive, as Mes now needs to compile the whole MesCC to bytecode. When running MesCC for longer, like in a real program (mescc-mes), shows the startup time is compensated by far by the execution speed.

In summary, we got exactly what we were aiming for: a change so big the benchmarks don’t need to be precise. An improvement you can just feel by running Mes.

When I wrote the bytecode compiler I added a very annoying warning that complained about possibly unbound variables when you did something like:

This was later removed because the amount of warnings it was producing was really overwhelming and they didn’t really give us any useful information.

But! When I tested the bootstrapping process during development I realized they appeared twice. This led me to find the build scripts were compiling each file twice by accident.

So now, we are not just x2 faster in Mes. The bootstrapping is also x2 faster thanks to the annoying warnings!

Comparing to the code in the earlier post in the series, the released code has proper support for values and call-with-values that I thought I did right but I didn’t, really.

According to R7RS standard, the values procedure returns its arguments as values to the current continuation. If the continuation only accepts one value, only the first value is sent to the continuation. That’s what a regular continuation would do. With call-with-values the producer is called in a continuation that accepts multiple values that go directly to the consumer procedure.

If you take a look to the Guile case, that’s exactly how it works. Chibi takes the pragmatic approach not implementing the value discard and uses values just as a container. That’s what I implemented in the previous blogpost, but in the release I managed to do the standards compliant case, and make a REPL that now supports multiple return values, like Guile does:

The tricky part of values is solved with a very primitive support for continuation marks.

When call-with-values is called, the current frame is labeled with a mark, saying it accepts multiple values. When values is called, it checks the current mark in order to decide if it should keep or discard its arguments. It looks like this:

This whole thing works very well thanks to proper tail-calls, which reuse the frames so the marks are right in the current frame all the time. It’s clean and simple.

It also uses the simplest approach possible. The %values builtin wraps values in a list, adding an special car to it. core:cdr can be used to extract the list of values back from the wrapper.

Of course, we could do this “better” just putting the values raw in the stack, but this is good enough for now. If Chibi can get away with doing less, we should be fine with this.

I would never solve this issue if it wasn’t because some random research I did, encouraged by Tim and all the knowledge he has about Scheme implementations.

I was looking at a few papers on delimited continuations, like “Final Shift for Call/cc: Direct Implementation of Shift and Reset” by Martin Gasbichler and Michael Sperber, when Tim told me about his approach in Germ using continuation marks.

With that in mind, I made a very fast sketch on how would continuation marks look like and I realized that was more than enough for the values implementation I was struggling with when I saw the Mes tests (which I didn’t bother to run during the research time) started to fail for the value discard case.

I ended up using only the most minimal thing for it, but I hope to take it a little bit further in the future and make a proper continuation marks based Delimited Continuation support for Mes.

There are many things happening in this release. The diff is huge. But mostly you have been following the effort during the latest blogposts so there’s no need to go deeply in detail.

You saw me re-write the garbage collector, the macro expander, the driver, the builtin implementation, vectors and structs, values, continuations … Some of the code is gone (gc, macro expander and driver, the first implementation of continuations) but the knowledge stays. I basically visited every single corner in this interpreter.

I’m used to hop from one thing to the next. That’s the R&D me again. Now that I know this software the best, I don’t want to just go do anything else. Now I’m the best position to improve it further.

My goal for the future is to improve Mes in all those areas that I found it could be improved but I couldn’t focus on.

Delimited continuations are the best way to represent continuations in an stack based VM like the one I added to Mes. They are more lightweight, better for the GC, and they are composable, allowing for more sophisticated control. Guile supports them, so it would also help us get a step closer to Guile.

Pointer tagging could be a huge deal for speed and reduced memory usage in contrast to the tagged union approach Mes has. To give you an example, in a 64 bit machine each value is at least 24 bytes, including characters. This means if you (string->list "Hello") the result takes 24 bytes per cons cell, i.e per element, plus 24 bytes per character. Pointer tagging would put the bytes for the characters inside the pointers the cons cells have, reducing the total memory to just what the list needs (half of the previous case) and removing the need to access memory again to get the value of the characters.

With some type punning we could also revisit a few data structures we had some trouble with (mostly frames and templates) and make them flat and easy for the CPU to cache and access with no indirection.

In the case of the Scheme to bytecode compiler, just making it slightly better than the dumbest thing possible can make Scheme code fly: builtin inlining, avoiding boxing of non-mutated values… There are many things we can do while keeping complexity under control.

Some GC improvement is also needed, maybe with a simple generational-style garbage collector (does that exist?), at least for a few things like symbols and globals that are never collected it could improve the performance. Even if it doesn’t, we could always use some cleanup in the GC, which is very error prone now.

Those are low-hanging fruits that the new architecture made more accessible. If I just stop here they could be lost.

On the mid term, with all this together and all the improvements Janneke is doing, we could bring MesCC to the next level as a C99 compiler written in Guile that can be incidentally run in Mes.

On the long term, the GNU Mes project would become a very powerful bootstrapping toolchain for languages of any kind.

The GNU Mes development repository is now hosted in Codeberg, under the Mes organization8:

And we have opened an IRC channel at libera.chat: #mes

I tend to listen to my heart, my curiosity, gut feeling, or whatever you want to call it. That has pushed me to do uncomfortable things.

It is daunting, but it has been really rewarding.

The same way Free Software has made me learn how to program, GNU Mes has been an amazing training camp for the skills I was lacking: reading CS papers, preparing a release, writing code from scratch…

The project made me understand slowing down is sometimes the best way to go forward, and that I have to be more comfortable switching gears.

This is not just programming advice, but a general approach to life that I’m starting to understand as I get older —and hopefully wiser.9

Thankfully I’m surrounded by people I can learn from, and they bring the best version of me. All the crazy things that I attempt would have been impossible without the people I find in the process.

In this specific case of Mes, I’m very happy with the team we have. They supported me throughout the whole process, but specially during the release, when I was more insecure. I’m sure the next time I’ll be more comfortable slowing down and doing things right.

Thanks to them for the help, inspiration and support.

Thanks to NlNet and NGI for the trust and the chance to work in important but not-very-popular projects. Without funding, none of this is possible.

I hope we can continue to work all together for some time more.

We closed this one well. There’s no reason to stop here, though.

The “GNU Mes speedup effort” project has been funded through NGI Zero Core, a fund established by NLnet with financial support from the European Commission’s Next Generation Internet program.

I have mixed feelings with it, really. From time to time I come back to it and I cannot figure out how to do it. Then something else comes and I have to leave it. It’s a shame. ↩

Of something I’ve never did before (an optimization work) in something that I never worked before (a scheme interpreter). ↩

The other possibility was to chicken out, give Janneke the branch and disappear. ↩

Also, getting an email by RMS himself congratulating me for the release has made me a little bit emotional. Not gonna lie. I’m sure he does that for every release, but I’m a weak man. ↩

Thanks to my friend Iban for the SSH access. Siuuuh! ↩

My repository has been transferred to Mes. ↩

I can’t wait to hear people say this post is written by AI because of the em-dashes. I’m putting them here and there just to mess with them. ↩
